## Learning goals

This book asks you to *run* economics, not only to read it. Everything happens in a web browser, and you
do not need to install anything. By the end of this appendix you will be able to:

- explain what **Google Colab** is, why this book uses it, and what its limits are;
- open any notebook of the book in Colab, run it, move its sliders, save your own copy and close it properly;
- write short **Python** programs with numbers, variables, lists, loops, `if` statements and functions,
  using examples from the book's models;
- load, explore and reshape a real data table with **pandas**, compute with **NumPy**, draw interactive
  charts with **Plotly**, and add sliders with **ipywidgets**;
- put these pieces together in a small data project: which economies grew fastest after 1990?

<!-- cell -->

## A.1 What is Google Colab?

A **notebook** is a document that mixes three things: text (like this paragraph), code, and the results
of that code (numbers, tables and charts). You read it from top to bottom. When you change a piece of code
and run it again, its result updates right below it. That makes notebooks a good way to learn, because the
explanation, the computation and the evidence sit side by side.

**Google Colab** (short for Colaboratory) is a free service from Google that runs notebooks inside your web
browser. The notebooks follow the open Jupyter format (`.ipynb` files), which is the standard in data science.
When you run a notebook in Colab, the code does not run on your laptop. It runs on a computer in one of
Google's data centres, called the **runtime**, and the results come back to your browser.

<!-- cell -->

### Why this book uses Colab

- **Nothing to install.** Python and all the libraries this book needs (NumPy, pandas, Plotly and
  ipywidgets) are already installed in Colab. You only need a web browser and a Google account.
- **The same setup for everyone.** Every reader runs the same versions of the same tools. Code that works
  for the author works for you, on Windows, macOS, Linux or a Chromebook.
- **Live models.** In Colab, the model figures of the book get sliders and buttons. Move a slider and the
  model is solved again on the spot.
- **Easy to save and share.** You can save your own copy of any notebook in Google Drive, and share it with a
  classmate or an instructor with a link, much like a Google Doc.
- **Data straight from the source.** Each notebook reads its data files over the internet from the book's
  GitHub repository, so you never have to download or upload a data file.

<!-- cell -->

### What to keep in mind

- **The runtime is temporary.** When you close the notebook, or leave it idle for a while, Colab disconnects
  the runtime and forgets every variable. Free sessions also have a maximum length of several hours (see
  the [Colab FAQ](https://research.google.com/colaboratory/faq.html)). This is not a problem for this book:
  click *Runtime → Run all* again and everything is rebuilt in a few seconds.
- **Your edits are not saved automatically** in a notebook you opened from GitHub. Save your own copy in
  Google Drive first (Section A.2, step 6).
- **Free resources are shared.** The free tier limits how many notebooks can run at the same time. Close a
  runtime properly when you are done (Section A.2, step 7).
- **You need to be online**, because the runtime and the data both live on the internet.

## A.3 Working in a notebook

A notebook is a list of **cells**. *Text cells* are written in Markdown, a simple way to format text
(`**bold**`, `*italic*`, `# Heading`), and they can hold equations such as $y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}$.
*Code cells* hold Python. To run a code cell, click inside it and press **Shift+Enter**, or click the round
▶ button at its left. Try it on the cell below.

```{python}
# A code cell: Python works out the expression and shows the result of the last line
2 + 3
```

Only the result of the **last line** of a cell is shown automatically. To show anything else, use `print`.

```{python}
print("Hello, Colab!")
x = 10
x * 2          # the last line: its value is shown below the cell
```

Screenshot A.10 shows the same idea in Colab: a new code cell with its result underneath. The number 70 in
brackets means it was the seventieth cell run in that session.

<img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/images/appA/colab-08-new-cell.png" width="760" alt="A code cell in Colab that computes 1.02 to the power 35 and shows the result 1.9998895526624565">

*Screenshot A.10. A new code cell and its result.*

<!-- cell -->

### The order of cells matters

A notebook remembers every variable you have created, in the order in which **you ran** the cells, not the
order in which they appear on the page. The next two cells work only if you run the first one before the
second. If you open a notebook and run a cell in the middle, you may see a `NameError` (Section A.4.8),
because a cell above it has not run yet. The cure is almost always *Runtime → Run all*, or *Runtime → Run
before* followed by the cell itself.

```{python}
interest_rate = 0.05          # create a variable...
```

```{python}
interest_rate * 100           # ...and use it in a later cell
```

<!-- cell -->

## A.4 Python fundamentals

Python is a programming language that reads almost like English. This section covers the handful of ideas
you need for the whole book. Every example comes from the economics of the book.

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.1 Numbers and arithmetic

Python works like a calculator. `**` raises a number to a power, which is all you need for compound growth.

```{python}
print(7 + 3, 7 - 3, 7 * 3, 7 / 3)     # add, subtract, multiply, divide
print(7 // 3, 7 % 3)                 # whole-number division and its remainder
print(2 ** 10)                       # a power: 2 to the 10th
```

An economy that grows at 2 percent a year is multiplied by 1.02 every year. After 35 years it is
$1.02^{35}$ times as large:

```{python}
1.02 ** 35
```

It has almost exactly doubled. This is the *rule of 70* of Chapter 3 at work: at 2 percent a year, a
variable doubles in about 70/2 = 35 years.

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.2 Variables

A **variable** is a name for a value. The `=` sign means "store the value on the right under the name on the
left". Names may contain letters, digits and underscores, but not spaces, and they are case-sensitive
(`GDP` and `gdp` are different names). In this book the names follow the notation of the textbook, such as
`s`, `d`, `A`, `k_star` and `y_star`.

```{python}
y_1990 = 47713      # U.S. GDP per person in 1990, 2022 dollars (Maddison data, Section A.5)
y_2022 = 75459      # the same in 2022
growth_factor = y_2022 / y_1990
growth_factor
```

From the growth factor we get the **average annual growth rate**: the rate $g$ that turns $y_{1990}$ into
$y_{2022}$ in 32 years, $y_{2022} = y_{1990}(1+g)^{32}$, so $g = (y_{2022}/y_{1990})^{1/32} - 1$.

```{python}
g = growth_factor ** (1 / 32) - 1
g
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.3 Types of values and f-strings

Every value has a **type**. The four you will meet most are whole numbers (`int`), decimal numbers
(`float`), text (`str`, for *string*, written in quotes) and truth values (`bool`: `True` or `False`).

```{python}
country = "United States"           # a string
years = 2022 - 1990                 # an int
g = growth_factor ** (1 / years) - 1    # a float
is_rich = y_2022 > 50000            # a bool, the result of a comparison
print(type(country), type(years), type(g), type(is_rich))
```

> **Python note.** An **f-string** is a string with an `f` before the opening quote. Python replaces each
> `{...}` inside it with the value of the expression. After a colon you can set the format: `{g:.2%}` shows
> `g` as a percentage with 2 decimals, `{y:,.0f}` shows `y` with a thousands separator and no decimals.

```{python}
print(f"{country}: GDP per person grew from {y_1990:,.0f} to {y_2022:,.0f} dollars,")
print(f"or {g:.2%} a year on average over {years} years.")
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.4 Lists and loops

A **list** holds several values in order, inside square brackets. Python counts positions from **0**, so
`countries[0]` is the first element and `countries[-1]` the last one.

```{python}
countries = ["United States", "Japan", "China"]
print(countries[0], "|", countries[-1], "|", len(countries), "countries")
countries.append("India")        # add an element at the end
countries
```

A **`for` loop** repeats the indented lines below it, once for each value. `range(1, 6)` gives the
whole numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Note the colon at the end of the `for` line and the four spaces of
indentation: they tell Python which lines belong to the loop.

```{python}
# Compound growth, year by year: income grows by 2 percent each year
y = 100.0
for year in range(1, 6):
    y = y * 1.02
    print(f"year {year}: {y:.2f}")
```

Loops are how the book simulates models over time. Here is the capital accumulation equation of the Solow
model (Chapter 5), $k_{t+1} = k_t + s\,k_t^{1/3} - d\,k_t$, run for 50 years. Each year, capital per person
grows by investment and shrinks by depreciation.

```{python}
s, d = 0.2, 0.1        # investment rate and depreciation rate
k = 1.0                # capital per person in year 0
path = [k]             # a list that will hold the whole path
for t in range(50):
    k = k + s * k ** (1 / 3) - d * k
    path.append(k)
k_star = (s / d) ** 1.5                 # the steady state of this model, (s/d)^(3/2)
print(f"k after 10 years: {path[10]:.3f}, after 50 years: {path[50]:.3f}")
print(f"steady state k* = {k_star:.3f}")
```

Capital rises quickly at first and then slows down as it approaches the steady state: the *principle of
transition dynamics* of Chapter 5.

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.5 Making decisions with `if`

`if`, `elif` (else if) and `else` run different lines depending on a condition. The comparisons are `>`,
`<`, `>=`, `<=`, `==` (equal; note the double sign) and `!=` (not equal).

```{python}
g_percent = 1.4                  # an average growth rate, in percent a year
if g_percent >= 3:
    label = "fast"
elif g_percent >= 1:
    label = "moderate"
else:
    label = "slow or negative"
print(f"Growth of {g_percent}% a year is {label}.")
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.6 Dictionaries

A **dictionary** stores values under names (*keys*), inside curly braces. The book uses dictionaries for
sets of parameters and for colors.

```{python}
params = {"s": 0.2, "d": 0.1, "A": 1.0}
print(params["s"])               # look up a value by its key
params["s"] = 0.3                # change it
for key in params:
    print(key, "=", params[key])
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.7 Functions

A **function** packs a few lines of code under a name, so you can reuse them. `def` starts the definition,
the names in parentheses are its *arguments*, and `return` sends back the result. An argument with a
default value (`A=1.0`) can be left out when you call the function. The text in triple quotes, the
*docstring*, says what the function does. In the chapters each model equation becomes one short function
like this one, the production function of Chapter 4.

```{python}
def output(k, A=1.0):
    """Output per person in the production model of Chapter 4: y = A k^(1/3)."""
    return A * k ** (1 / 3)

print(output(8))           # k = 8 and the default A = 1
print(output(8, A=2.0))    # the same capital with twice the productivity
```

A second function turns the rule of 70 into code and uses a loop to try several growth rates.

```{python}
def years_to_double(g_percent):
    """Rule of 70 (Chapter 3): something growing at g percent a year doubles in about 70/g years."""
    return 70 / g_percent

for g_percent in [1, 2, 3.5, 7]:
    print(f"growth of {g_percent}% a year: doubles in about {years_to_double(g_percent):.0f} years")
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.4.8 Libraries and errors

A **library** (or *package*) is a collection of functions that someone else has written. `import` loads
one. The built-in `math` library, for example, has the natural logarithm, which gives the exact doubling
time $\ln 2 / \ln(1+g)$ to compare with the rule of 70. The rule is very close at low growth rates and a
little off at high ones.

```{python}
import math
for g_percent in [2, 7]:
    exact = math.log(2) / math.log(1 + g_percent / 100)
    rule = years_to_double(g_percent)
    print(f"At {g_percent}% a year: exactly {exact:.1f} years; rule of 70: {rule:.1f} years")
```

Everyone writes code with mistakes. When Python cannot run a line, it stops and prints an **error message**
(a *traceback*). Read it from the **bottom**: the last line names the kind of error and what went wrong, and
an arrow `---->` points to the line that failed. Screenshot A.11 shows a typo in a variable name, which gives a
`NameError`. Colab may also offer an *Explain error* button that asks Google's AI assistant for an
explanation. It can help, but read its answer critically.

<img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/images/appA/colab-09-error.png" width="760" alt="A Colab cell with a typo, grwoth instead of growth, and the resulting NameError message">

*Screenshot A.11. A `NameError`: the variable `grwoth` was never created (the name is `growth`).*

<!-- cell -->

You can also catch an error yourself with `try ... except`. Python tries the indented lines under `try`; if
they fail with the named error, it runs the lines under `except` instead of stopping. The setup cell of every
chapter uses this to run one line that only works in Colab.

```{python}
try:
    "GDP in " + 2025          # text plus a number: Python refuses to guess what you mean
except TypeError as error:
    print("TypeError:", error)
print("GDP in " + str(2025))    # the fix: turn the number into text first
```

## A.5 The data science libraries of this book

Four libraries do almost all the work in this book. Every chapter uses all four.

| Library | Nickname | What it does | Where you will see it most |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NumPy** | `np` | fast math on whole arrays of numbers | model curves (`np.linspace`), logs, fitted trend lines (`np.polyfit`, in Chapters 2, 9, 12, 19 and 21) |
| **pandas** | `pd` | data tables: read, filter, reshape, combine | every data figure; `groupby` in 19 chapters, `merge` in 12, `pivot` in 10 |
| **Plotly** | `px`, `go` | interactive charts: hover, zoom, legends, sliders, animations | Plotly Express (`px`) for data figures; `graph_objects` (`go`) for model figures; `make_subplots` for two-panel figures in 9 chapters |
| **ipywidgets** | — | sliders, buttons and menus that rerun a function | the live model figures and the country pickers of the data figures |

<!-- cell -->

### A.5.1 The setup cell

Every chapter starts with a **setup cell** like the one below. It loads the libraries, sets one light
blue/green look for all charts, switches on Colab's support for interactive charts, and stores the web
address of the chapter's data files in `DATA_URL`. You only need to run it once per session, but it must run
before anything else, which *Run all* takes care of.

> **Python note.** `import numpy as np` loads NumPy and gives it the nickname `np`, so we can write
> `np.log` instead of `numpy.log`. `from ipywidgets import interact` loads one function from a library, so
> we can write just `interact`. Names in capital letters, such as `BLUE` or `DATA_URL`, are a convention
> for constants: values we set once and never change.

```{python}
# Libraries used in this appendix
import numpy as np                              # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                             # data tables
import plotly.express as px                     # quick charts from data tables
import plotly.graph_objects as go               # charts built piece by piece (model figures)
import plotly.io as pio
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots       # several panels in one figure
from ipywidgets import interact, FloatSlider, Dropdown, SelectMultiple

# One light blue/green look for every chart
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3"
pio.templates.default = "plotly_white"
pio.templates["plotly_white"].layout.update(width=860, height=480)   # same size in Colab and on the website
px.defaults.color_discrete_sequence = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, "#c4651a", "#8e5ea2", "#5aa0d8", "#0b4f47"]
WIDE = {"description_width": "initial"}         # show the full widget labels

# Colab only: let Plotly charts appear inside the interactive widgets
try:
    import google.colab
    google.colab.output.enable_custom_widget_manager()
except ImportError:
    pass                                        # not running in Colab: nothing to do

# The data files of this appendix live in the book's GitHub repository
DATA_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/main/data/appA/"
```

Most chapters also have one or two folded **helper cells** right after the setup cell. They build the
website versions of the interactive figures. Run them and move on.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Precompute make_figure(name=value) for every value and join the results with one slider.

    The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets this precomputed version.
    """
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                                  # which precomputed figure each trace comes from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.5.2 NumPy: math on whole arrays

A NumPy **array** is like a list of numbers, but you can do math on all its elements at once, without a
loop. `np.linspace(start, stop, n)` makes `n` evenly spaced numbers. The chapters use it to make the
x-values of every model curve.

```{python}
k = np.linspace(0, 10, 6)        # 6 evenly spaced values from 0 to 10
print(k)
print(k ** (1 / 3))              # the cube root of every element at once
print(output(k))                 # our function from A.4.7 works on a whole array too
```

NumPy also has the usual math functions and summaries: `np.log` (natural log), `np.exp`, `np.sqrt`, and
`.mean()`, `.max()` and `.min()` on an array.

```{python}
growth_rates = np.array([1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0])
print(growth_rates.mean(), growth_rates.max())
print(np.log(100), np.exp(np.log(100)))      # exp undoes log
```

<!-- cell -->

### A.5.3 pandas: data tables

pandas stores data in a **DataFrame**: a table with named columns and one row per observation.
`pd.read_csv` reads a CSV file (comma-separated values, the simplest spreadsheet format) from your computer
or, as here, from a web address. Our first file holds GDP per person for seven countries since 1870, from the
Maddison Project Database. `.head()` shows the first five rows.

```{python}
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "maddison_panel.csv")
panel.head()
```

The table is in **long** (or *tidy*) format: one row per country and year. `iso3` is a three-letter
country code, and `gdppc` is GDP per person in 2022 U.S. dollars. Three quick ways to look at a new table:

```{python}
print(panel.shape)                 # (number of rows, number of columns)
print(panel.columns.tolist())      # the column names
panel.describe()                   # count, mean, min, max ... of each numeric column
```

<!-- cell -->

#### Selecting and filtering

`panel["country"]` picks one column. Putting a condition inside the brackets keeps only the rows where it
is `True`. Combine conditions with `&` (and) or `|` (or), each inside its own parentheses.

```{python}
japan = panel[panel["country"] == "Japan"]           # keep only Japan's rows
japan.tail(3)                                        # .tail shows the last rows
```

```{python}
asia = panel[(panel["year"] >= 2018) & (panel["country"].isin(["China", "India"]))]
asia
```

<!-- cell -->

#### New columns, sorting and summaries by group

You create a new column by assigning to it. `sort_values` sorts the rows, and `groupby` splits the table
into groups, here one per country, and summarizes each group.

```{python}
panel["gdppc_thousands"] = panel["gdppc"] / 1000      # GDP per person in thousands of dollars
latest = panel[panel["year"] == 2022]
latest.sort_values("gdppc", ascending=False)
```

```{python}
panel.groupby("country")["gdppc"].agg(["min", "max", "count"])
```

The `count` column already tells a story about the data: the United States and the United Kingdom have all
153 years from 1870 to 2022, but China has only 89, because the historical estimates for China cover only
some of the years before 1950.

<!-- cell -->

#### Reshaping with `pivot`, and missing values

`pivot` turns the long table into a **wide** one, with one row per year and one column per country. Years
with no estimate become `NaN` ("not a number"), pandas' marker for a missing value. `.loc[...]` picks rows
by their label, here by year.

```{python}
wide = panel.pivot(index="year", columns="country", values="gdppc")
print(wide.isna().sum())              # missing years in each column
wide.loc[[1870, 1950, 2022]]
```

With the wide table, the average annual growth rate of every country since 1950 takes one line, the
formula of Section A.4.2 applied to whole columns at once:

```{python}
growth_since_1950 = ((wide.loc[2022] / wide.loc[1950]) ** (1 / 72) - 1) * 100
growth_since_1950.sort_values().round(2)
```

<!-- cell -->

#### Combining tables with `merge`

Often the information you need sits in two tables. Our second file has, for 111 countries, GDP per person
in 2023 relative to the United States and the average growth rate from 1960 to 2023, from the Penn World
Table. A third file lists each country's World Bank region and income group. `merge` joins them on the
column they share, the country code `iso3`.

```{python}
growth60 = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "fig3-7.csv")
names = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
growth60 = growth60.merge(names[["iso3", "region", "income"]], on="iso3", how="left")
growth60.head()
```

```{python}
growth60.groupby("region")["growth_1960_2023_pct"].mean().sort_values().round(2)
```

### A.5.4 Plotly Express: charts from data tables

**Plotly Express** (`px`) draws a whole chart from a DataFrame in one call: you name the table and say which
column goes on each axis and which column sets the colors. The charts are interactive. Hover over a line to
read its values, drag to zoom, double-click to zoom back out, and click a legend entry to hide or show that
country.

```{python}
fig = px.line(panel, x="year", y="gdppc", color="country", log_y=True,
              labels={"year": "Year", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars, ratio scale)",
                      "country": ""},
              title="GDP per person in seven economies, 1870-2022")
fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000])
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024), GDP per person converted to 2022 dollars.
Prepared file: [`data/appA/maddison_panel.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/maddison_panel.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by the discussion of long-run growth in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024),
[*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

> **Python note.** `log_y=True` puts the y-axis on a **ratio (log) scale**: equal distances mean equal
> percentage changes, so a straight line means a constant growth rate. Chapter 3 explains why economists
> prefer it for long-run data. `tickvals` chooses which numbers label the axis.

<!-- cell -->

A scatter plot with `px.scatter` shows how two variables relate. `hover_name="country"` puts the country
name in the box that appears when you hover over a point, and `color="region"` gives each region its own color.
We first drop Venezuela, whose PWT GDP per person after 2017 is not plausible: hyperinflation broke the price
data (Chapter 3 discusses this).

```{python}
plot_data = growth60[growth60["iso3"] != "VEN"]
labels = {"gdppc_rel_us_2023": "GDP per person in 2023 (U.S. = 1, ratio scale)",
          "growth_1960_2023_pct": "Average growth, 1960-2023 (percent a year)",
          "region": "Region"}
fig = px.scatter(plot_data, x="gdppc_rel_us_2023", y="growth_1960_2023_pct", color="region",
                 hover_name="country", log_x=True, labels=labels,
                 title="Countries that grew faster since 1960 are richer today")
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=[0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1])
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) (Feenstra, Inklaar and
Timmer 2015), real GDP per person (`rgdpe`/`pop`); regions from the
[World Bank country classification](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519).
Prepared files: [`data/appA/fig3-7.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/fig3-7.csv) and
[`data/appA/countries.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/countries.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 3.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

`animation_frame` turns a column into a **play button and a slider**: each frame of the animation shows the
rows for one value of that column. `range_y` fixes the y-axis, so that the bars can grow from frame to frame.

```{python}
decades = panel[panel["year"].isin([1950, 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020])]
fig = px.bar(decades, x="country", y="gdppc", animation_frame="year", range_y=[0, 80000],
             labels={"country": "", "gdppc": "GDP per person (2022 dollars)", "year": "Year"},
             title="GDP per person by decade: press the play button")
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024). Prepared file: [`data/appA/maddison_panel.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/maddison_panel.csv).
Chart: inspired by the discussion of long-run growth in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

**What to notice.** China's bar barely moves until 1980 and then rises faster than any other. By 2020 it
has passed Argentina and South Africa.

### A.5.5 Plotly graph objects: charts built piece by piece

For model figures we want full control: which curves, which colors, which labels. **Plotly graph objects**
(`go`) build a chart step by step. `go.Figure()` starts an empty chart, each `add_trace` adds one curve, and
`update_layout` sets the title and the axes. Here are two production functions $y = \bar{A}k^{1/3}$ from
Chapter 4, drawn with the `output` function of Section A.4.7.

```{python}
k = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k), mode="lines", name="A = 1",
                         line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=output(k, A=1.5), mode="lines", name="A = 1.5",
                         line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3, dash="dash")))
fig.update_layout(title="Higher productivity A shifts the production function up",
                  xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 10],
                             tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                  yaxis=dict(title="Output per person, y", range=[0, 3.5]))
fig.show()
```

**Source.** Adapted from the production model of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024),
[*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

`make_subplots` puts several panels side by side. The two panels below show the same data on a linear scale
and on a ratio scale. On the linear scale, U.S. growth seems to speed up over time. On the ratio scale, the
U.S. line is close to straight: its *percentage* growth has been fairly steady. China's line bends upward
after 1980.

> **Python note.** The loop runs once for each `(name, color)` pair in the list. `row=` and `col=` say which
> panel a trace goes to, and `showlegend=False` keeps each country only once in the legend.

```{python}
fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2, subplot_titles=("Linear scale", "Ratio scale"))
for name, color in [("United States", BLUE), ("China", TEAL)]:
    one = panel[panel["country"] == name]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=one["year"], y=one["gdppc"], mode="lines", name=name,
                             line=dict(color=color)), row=1, col=1)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=one["year"], y=one["gdppc"], mode="lines", name=name,
                             line=dict(color=color), showlegend=False), row=1, col=2)
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="GDP per person (2022 dollars)", row=1, col=1)
fig.update_yaxes(type="log", tickvals=[1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000], row=1, col=2)
fig.update_layout(title="The same two series on two scales")
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Maddison Project Database 2023](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/historicaldevelopment/maddison/releases/maddison-project-database-2023)
(Bolt and van Zanden 2024). Prepared file: [`data/appA/maddison_panel.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/maddison_panel.csv).
Chart: inspired by the discussion of ratio scales in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

### A.5.6 ipywidgets: sliders and menus

**ipywidgets** turns the arguments of a function into controls. `interact(f, ...)` draws one control for
each argument and calls `f` again every time you move one. This is how every model figure in the book becomes
interactive: we write a function that returns a figure, and hand it to `interact`.

```{python}
def production_figure(A=1.0, alpha=1 / 3):
    """Production function y = A k^alpha (Chapter 4), with fixed axes so changes are visible."""
    k = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
    fig = go.Figure()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=k ** (1 / 3), mode="lines", name="Baseline: A = 1, α = 1/3",
                             line=dict(color=GRAY, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=k, y=A * k ** alpha, mode="lines", name="Your production function",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"Output per person at k = 8: y = {A * 8 ** alpha:.2f} (baseline 2.00)",
                      xaxis=dict(title="Capital per person, k", range=[0, 10],
                                 tickvals=[2, 4, 6, 8, 10]),
                      yaxis=dict(title="Output per person, y", range=[0, 7]))
    return fig
```

> **Python note.** `FloatSlider` makes a slider for decimal numbers, from `min` to `max` in steps of
> `step`, starting at `value`. `Dropdown` makes a menu; each option is a pair `("label shown", value)`.
> `style=WIDE` shows the whole description. The `;` at the end hides an extra line of text.

```{python}
#| kind: widget
A_slider = FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.5, max=2.0, step=0.1,
                       description="productivity A", style=WIDE)
alpha_menu = Dropdown(options=[("1/4", 0.25), ("1/3", 1 / 3), ("1/2", 0.5)], value=1 / 3,
                      description="capital exponent α", style=WIDE)
interact(production_figure, A=A_slider, alpha=alpha_menu);
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: the production function with a precomputed slider for A
slider_figure(production_figure, "A", [0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0], start=1.0, label="productivity A")
```

**Source.** Adapted from the production model of Chapter 4 in Jones (2024),
[*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

**What to notice.** Doubling $\bar{A}$ doubles output at every level of capital. A larger exponent $\alpha$
makes the curve bend less, so diminishing returns to capital set in more slowly.

The chapters use a few more kinds of controls:

| Control | What it does | Example in the book |
|---|---|---|
| `FloatSlider`, `IntSlider` | choose a number | the investment rate in the Solow model (Chapter 5) |
| `Dropdown` | choose one option from a menu | a country or a base year |
| `ToggleButtons` | switch between a few options | linear or ratio scale |
| `SelectMultiple` | choose several items from a list | the country pickers of the data figures |
| `interact_manual` | run only when you press a button | the "Earthquake!" button of Chapter 5 |

## A.6 Putting it together: which economies grew fastest after 1990?

Our mini project uses every tool of this appendix. The question: which economies raised their GDP per
person fastest between 1990 and 2023, and which fell behind? The data come from the Penn World Table, with
one row per economy and year from 1950 to 2023.

**Step 1: load and look.**

```{python}
pwt = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_income.csv")
print(pwt.shape, "|", pwt["country"].nunique(), "economies")
print("years:", pwt["year"].min(), "to", pwt["year"].max())
pwt.head()
```

<!-- cell -->

**Step 2: one row per economy with its 1990 and 2023 values.** We filter each year, keep the columns we need
and `merge` the two tables on the country code. `suffixes` tells pandas how to rename the two `gdp_pc`
columns. Then we apply the growth formula to whole columns at once.

```{python}
start = pwt[pwt["year"] == 1990][["iso3", "country", "gdp_pc"]]
end = pwt[pwt["year"] == 2023][["iso3", "gdp_pc"]]
both = start.merge(end, on="iso3", suffixes=("_1990", "_2023"))
both["growth"] = ((both["gdp_pc_2023"] / both["gdp_pc_1990"]) ** (1 / 33) - 1) * 100
print(len(both), "economies have data in both years")
both.sort_values("growth").head(3)
```

**Step 3: look at your data.** The slowest "grower" is Venezuela, at about −13 percent a year. As in the
chapters, that number is not plausible: hyperinflation broke the PWT price data after 2017. We drop it and
then list the five fastest and five slowest economies, adding the doubling time from our rule-of-70 function.

```{python}
both = both[both["iso3"] != "VEN"]
fastest = both.nlargest(5, "growth")
slowest = both.nsmallest(5, "growth")
fastest["doubles_in_years"] = years_to_double(fastest["growth"]).round(0)
columns = ["country", "gdp_pc_1990", "gdp_pc_2023", "growth"]
print("Fastest growth, 1990-2023 (percent a year):")
print(fastest[columns + ["doubles_in_years"]].round(1).to_string(index=False))
print("\nSlowest growth:")
print(slowest[columns].round(1).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\n{(both['growth'] < 0).sum()} of {len(both)} economies were poorer in 2023 than in 1990.")
```

**What to notice.**

- China grew at 7.6 percent a year: at that pace income doubles about every nine years, and it rose more
  than tenfold in 33 years.
- Guyana tops the list because of oil: production from its offshore oil fields began in 2019. Fast growth
  of GDP per person can come from a resource boom, not only from capital and ideas.
- Twelve economies were poorer in 2023 than in 1990, among them Zimbabwe, Tajikistan and the United Arab
  Emirates. In the Emirates, total GDP grew about 3.7 times, but the population grew 5.6 times, from 1.9 to
  10.6 million, so GDP *per person* fell.

<!-- cell -->

**Step 4: an interactive chart.** Our last function draws GDP per person over time for any economies you
pick, on a ratio scale. In Colab, hold Ctrl (⌘ on a Mac) and click names in the list to choose several.

```{python}
def growth_figure(names=("China", "United States", "Zimbabwe")):
    """GDP per person since 1950 for the chosen economies, on a ratio scale."""
    chosen = pwt[pwt["country"].isin(names)]
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdp_pc", color="country", log_y=True,
                  range_x=[1950, 2023], range_y=[80, 400000],     # every value fits
                  labels={"year": "Year", "gdp_pc": "GDP per person (2021 dollars, ratio scale)",
                          "country": ""},
                  title=f"GDP per person since 1950: {len(names)} economies")
    fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=[100, 300, 1000, 3000, 10000, 30000, 100000, 300000])
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
all_names = sorted(pwt["country"].unique())
picker = SelectMultiple(options=all_names, value=("China", "United States", "Zimbabwe"),
                        rows=8, description="economies", style=WIDE)
interact(growth_figure, names=picker);
```

```{python}
#| kind: website
# @title Website version: the fastest and slowest growers, with buttons
groups = {"Fastest five": list(fastest["country"]), "Slowest five": list(slowest["country"])}
shown = groups["Fastest five"] + groups["Slowest five"] + ["United States"]
fig = growth_figure(names=shown)
buttons = []
for label, members in groups.items():
    visible = [(t.name in members) or (t.name == "United States") for t in fig.data]
    buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
buttons.append(dict(label="All eleven", method="update", args=[{"visible": [True] * len(fig.data)}]))
for t in fig.data:
    t.visible = (t.name in groups["Fastest five"]) or (t.name == "United States")
fig.update_layout(title="GDP per person since 1950: the fastest and slowest growers of 1990-2023",
                  updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", buttons=buttons, direction="right", x=0, y=1.02,
                                    xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")], margin=dict(t=120))
fig
```

**Sources.** Data: [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) (Feenstra, Inklaar and
Timmer 2015), real GDP per person (`rgdpe`/`pop`) in 2021 dollars.
Prepared file: [`data/appA/pwt_income.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/pwt_income.csv)
(see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/appA/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by the growth comparisons in Chapter 3 of Jones (2024),
[*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

On the website, use the buttons above the chart to switch between the fastest and the slowest growers (the
United States is always shown for comparison), and click a legend entry to hide or show one economy.

## A.7 Going further

<!-- cell -->

### Common errors and how to fix them

| Error message | What it usually means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `NameError: name 'x' is not defined` | a typo, or the cell that creates `x` has not run yet | check the spelling; *Runtime → Run before* |
| `TypeError: can only concatenate str ...` | mixing text and numbers | convert with `str(...)` or use an f-string |
| `KeyError: 'gdp'` | a column name that does not exist | print `df.columns` and copy the exact name |
| `IndentationError` | the spaces at the start of a line are wrong | indent the body of `for`, `if` and `def` by 4 spaces |
| `SyntaxError` | a missing bracket, quote or colon | look at the line marked by the arrow and the one before it |
| `HTTPError: HTTP Error 404` | a data file name or web address is wrong | check the file name after `DATA_URL` |
| `ModuleNotFoundError` | a library is not installed | in Colab, run `%pip install name` in a cell; the chapters never need it, but Appendix B does |

## Concluding remarks

- Google Colab runs Jupyter notebooks in your browser on Google's computers. It needs no installation, and it
  gives every reader the same tools. Run a notebook with *Runtime → Run all*, save your own copy in Drive,
  and delete the runtime when you are done.
- Python's basic building blocks are numbers and `**` for growth, variables, lists, `for` loops, `if`
  statements, dictionaries and functions. In this book each model equation becomes one short function.
- NumPy computes on whole arrays; pandas reads, filters, groups, pivots and merges data tables; Plotly draws
  interactive charts; ipywidgets adds sliders and menus that rerun a function.
- Read error messages from the bottom up. Most errors in notebooks come from typos or cells run out of order.
